title: Emulation of Entanglement Distribution Networks on a Quantum Computer
authors: Ashley N. Tittelbaugh, Jerry Horgan, Rohan Bali, Marco Ruffini, Daniel C. Kilper, Shelbi L. Jenkins, Boulat A. Bash
abstract: We investigate how quantum computers can be used to emulate quantum networks and study their performance under practical impairments. In particular, we evaluate how degraded entanglement and communication latency affect teleportation-based distributed multipartite-entanglement-state construction. We model imperfect Bell-pair sources using depolarizing noise channels and classical communication delays using thermal relaxation. We implement the depolarization using Stinespring dilation, randomly applied Pauli errors, and quasi-probability decompositions, evaluating the latter two on IQM quantum hardware and all three in simulation. We then study the performance of the entanglement distribution under noise generated by the aforementioned models. Although these noise models are mathematically equivalent, we find that hardware constraints result in profound differences in the corresponding results, highlighting the importance of careful experiment design.
summary: This paper models entanglement distribution across simulated and real quantum networks to build multipartite graph states. It rigorously tests the impact of noise sources, including depolarizing channels and classical communication delays, on network fidelity. The work is important because it demonstrates that hardware implementation details can drastically alter expected performance compared to idealized theoretical models.
main_problem: The study investigates how quantum computers can emulate complex quantum networks and assess their performance when subjected to practical noise sources like degraded entanglement and communication latency.
main_result: Hardware constraints lead to profound differences in results compared to simulations, highlighting that the choice of error model (e.g., QPD vs. Pauli) significantly impacts achievable network fidelity.
method: The authors modeled imperfect Bell-pair sources using depolarizing noise and classical delays by implementing various depolarization channels (Stinespring dilation, random Pauli errors, QPD).
model_or_system: The system involves emulating entanglement distribution networks to construct multipartite graph states, tested on superconducting quantum hardware (IQM Emerald) and in simulation.
key_observables: Bipartite-entanglement fidelity, stabilizer expectations for the resulting graph state, and the required network-distributed entanglement fidelity ($\ge 90\%$).
important_parameters: Classical communication delay (tested up to 10 ns and conceptually up to tens of kilometers); initial ZALM source fidelity (e.g., 99.6%).
main_assumptions: The study assumes mathematical equivalence between noise models but finds hardware implementation introduces discrepancies; rate investigation is left for future work.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ring graph state structure and circuit, compare stabilizer values across different depolarization channels (simulation vs. hardware), show fidelity sweeps versus network-distributed entanglement, and map fidelity loss against classical delay.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the problem of noisy quantum networking, detailing multiple noise models for Bell pairs, presenting comparative results on graph state construction fidelity under these noises, and finally discussing the implications of hardware vs. simulation discrepancies.
why_interesting: It provides concrete benchmarks for resource estimation in distributed quantum computing architectures, which is crucial for theorists designing fault-tolerant protocols that must account for realistic physical constraints.
